extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of humor theory, literary critics, and philosophers of art
extracted.subtask_description: A theoretical framework for identifying what makes something comic and what provokes laughter, emphasizing mechanisms such as rigidity, automatism, imitation, disguise, caricature, repetition, and the machine-like aspects of human life and social form. Useful for analysis or creation of comic effects in literature, performance, and social satire.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laughter as a social corrective
rubrics_metrics.description: Laughter is a social gesture that, by the fear which it inspires, restrains eccentricity and softens whatever the surface of the social body may retain of mechanical inelasticity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Laughter functions utilitarianly to promote sociability and mutual adaptation; it is social, not merely aesthetic. Example: laughter keeps secondary activities from 'retiring into their shell' and moderates inelasticity of character that could threaten social cohesion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic arises from rigidity/inelasticity
rubrics_metrics.description: The comic is associated with a certain rigidity of body, mind and character — an inelasticity that society would like to get rid of to achieve greater elasticity and sociability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrast comic with gracefulness rather than mere ugliness: the comic partakes of the unsprightly and of rigidness. Situations or people who suggest fixed, stereotyped, or petrified behaviour are comic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imitatability of deformity
rubrics_metrics.description: A deformity that may become comic is a deformity that a normally built person could successfully imitate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a hunchback suggests a posture that a non-deformed person can adopt, that suggestion (imitability) makes it comic. Use imitation tests to judge whether a physical trait can be comic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fixed, permanent grimace (comic physiognomy)
rubrics_metrics.description: A laughable expression of the face is one that promises nothing more than it gives: it is a unique and permanent grimace, as though the person's whole moral life had crystallised into that cast of features.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comic faces suggest a simple mechanical action into which personality would be absorbed (e.g., always weeping, always laughing). The more the face suggests a single mechanical action, the more comic it is.

rubrics_metrics.name: Automatism and contracted habit
rubrics_metrics.description: Automatism, inelasticity, and habit that has been contracted and maintained are clear causes why a face or action makes us laugh; the effect intensifies when linked to deep-seated absentmindedness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for signs that life has reverted to mechanical routine or a habitual, stereotyped action — that 'the soul had allowed itself to be fascinated ... by the materiality of a simple action.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Caricature principle: exaggeration revealing latent tendencies
rubrics_metrics.description: The caricaturist detects imperceptible tendencies in a face or form and renders them visible by magnifying them; exaggeration is comic only when used as a means to make manifest distortions seen in embryo, not as an end in itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective caricature lengthens or emphasizes features in the direction nature was already inclining (respecting the 'ground plan'), so the result appears as the subject's own exaggerated tendency rather than arbitrary distortion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gestures and movements are comic to the extent they suggest a machine
rubrics_metrics.description: The attitudes, gestures and movements of the human body are laughable in exact proportion as that body reminds us of a mere machine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate comic movement by how clearly and subtly it enables us to perceive a man as a jointed puppet: the clearer the internal 'set-up' mechanism appears while preserving an outward living aspect, the stronger the comic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repetition and imitation produce comic effect
rubrics_metrics.description: A movement always the same, returning at regular intervals, or gestures faithfully imitated by another, are laughable because they suggest automatism: repetition makes us see a machine working inside the living person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: a public speaker who repeats the same gesture or two faces that are too alike; imitation exposes the mechanical uniformity that is 'alien to our living personality' and thus provokes laughter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Association with mechanical occupation enhances comic
rubrics_metrics.description: Imitating or deflecting gestures toward a simple mechanical occupation (sawing wood, striking an anvil) makes them appear more frankly mechanical and hence more laughable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parody should link a gesture to a simple operation to emphasize its intentional mechanicality; clowns have intuitively used this device.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mass uniformity (marionette effect) intensifies comic
rubrics_metrics.description: When several characters simultaneously strike the same attitudes or toss their arms in the same manner, the uniformity makes them seem like marionettes and increases laughter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Group synchrony or mechanical sameness among performers amplifies the perception of automata (invisible threads), stiffening their 'litheness' into a puppet-like effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedic devices as clockwork arrangements
rubrics_metrics.description: Common devices of comedy (periodic repetition of a word/scene, inversion of parts, geometrical development of farce) derive comic force from presenting an obvious clockwork arrangement of human events while preserving an appearance of probability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Playwrights and comic writers create a visible mechanical scheme underlying events; the art lies in making the mechanism apparent but keeping enough 'supple' life for plausibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disguise and the illusion of artificiality
rubrics_metrics.description: A man in disguise, or anything regarded as disguised (hair dyed, a painted face), is comic because imagination treats the appearance as artificially laid on; the notion of disguise passes on comic quality to many cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: changing hair color, a rubicund nose (seen as painted vermilion), or perceiving a black face as 'unwashed' — the imagination's 'logic' reads these as masks or paint and finds them comic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fashion and discontinuity revealing comic quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Garments and fashions become laughable when they are no longer mentally fused with the individual; a break with continuity (old-fashioned dress, sudden novelty) revives the latent comic quality of fashion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Continuity and custom deaden comic potential; a dissolution of continuity or eccentric return to former fashions makes the clothing appear a disguise and thus comic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ceremony, formula, and stereotyped social actions as comic
rubrics_metrics.description: Any ceremony, form or formula becomes comic if attention is fixed on its ceremonial element and not its substantive purpose, because its stereotyped form suggests automatism and puppet-like motion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples range from prize-distributions to solemn court sittings; officials performing duties like mere machines or administrative regulations working with 'inexorable fatality' are comic targets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanical tampering with nature
rubrics_metrics.description: Nature that is mechanically tampered with (half-clipped dog, artificially coloured flowers, landscapes plastered with posters) provides comic themes because they suggest a masquerade or artificial overlay on the living.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The farther from the source, the weaker the comic element; to strengthen it, contrast the tampered image with the original living image (e.g., Jerome K. Jerome, Tartarin examples).

rubrics_metrics.name: Imaginative logic (dreamlike associative reasoning)
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a 'logic of the imagination' distinct from rational logic — a dreamlike chain of associations by which we accept absurd imaginative truths (e.g., 'a red nose is a painted nose') and which underlies many comic reactions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analysts should attend to these associative habits of imagination, which allow the mind to treat clothing, colour, or social forms as disguises and thereby produce comic effects; reconstructing this hidden logic requires lifting the crust of established ideas.
